title: Service lifetimes (singleton, scoped, transient)
hook: Every registered service has a lifetime — singleton (one for the app), scoped (one per request), or transient (new every resolution). Picking the wrong lifetime causes data leaks, thread-safety bugs, and the captive dependency trap.

blocks.text: Service lifetime controls how long the dependency injection (DI) container keeps an instance alive. ASP.NET Core supports three lifetimes: Singleton (one instance for the application lifetime), Scoped (one instance per scope — typically one HTTP request), and Transient (a new instance every time the service is resolved). AddSingleton, AddScoped, and AddTransient are the registration methods. Entity Framework Core DbContext is scoped by default — one context per request, disposed when the request ends.

entries.plainDefinition: One instance shared across the entire application. Thread-safe required if mutable state is shared.
One instance per scope. In web apps, a scope is created per HTTP request.
A new instance created every time the service is requested from the container.
The IServiceScope created at the start of each HTTP request and disposed at the end.
entries.example: HttpContext.RequestServices resolves from the per-request scope.

blocks.text: Lifetime choice is the #1 source of production DI bugs. Scoped DbContext in a singleton service means one database context forever — stale data, memory leaks, and ObjectDisposedException under concurrency. Transient services injected into singletons are also captured. Interviewers ask you to justify every lifetime choice: why is ICacheService singleton? Why is IOrderRepository scoped? Why is IValidator transient?

blocks.title: The golden rule
blocks.body: A service cannot depend on a shorter-lived service. Singleton → can only depend on singleton. Scoped → can depend on singleton or scoped. Transient → can depend on any lifetime, but each resolution creates new instances of its transient dependencies too.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Request starts
items.body: Kestrel creates an IServiceScope from the root provider.

items.title: Services resolved
items.body: Scoped services are created once per scope; singletons come from the root; transients are new each resolution.

items.title: Handler executes
items.body: Controller, minimal API handler, and middleware method-injected services share the same scoped instances.

items.title: Request ends
items.body: Scope.Dispose() runs — scoped services like DbContext are disposed.

snippet.label: Registering all three lifetimes
snippet.explanation: Cache is expensive to create and thread-safe — singleton. Repository shares DbContext per request — scoped. Template builder is stateless and cheap — transient. DbContext is always scoped.

snippet.label: Same scoped instance within one request
snippet.explanation: Multiple classes resolving ITenantContext in the same request get the identical instance. This is how per-request tenant isolation works without static state.

snippet.label: Transient vs scoped — when it matters
snippet.explanation: Transient is new per resolution — useful for stateless helpers. Scoped is new per scope — use when multiple components must share state within a request.

snippet.label: Diagnostics — scope disposal tracks active DbContext count
snippet.explanation: Monitor EF Core ActiveDbContexts with dotnet-counters. A steadily growing count under steady load indicates scoped services are not being disposed — usually a captive dependency.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Registering DbContext as singleton — never. Making a stateful service singleton without thread safety. Using transient for heavy services resolved many times per request (alloc pressure). Assuming IHttpClient is safe to new() — use IHttpClientFactory (singleton factory, managed handlers).

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: dotnet-counters Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore — ActiveDbContexts should equal concurrent in-flight requests. Steady growth means captive scoped services. Load test with k6 or NBomber — watch for ObjectDisposedException spikes indicating shared DbContext. OpenTelemetry spans showing overlapping DB operations on the same connection from different trace IDs = lifetime bug. ValidateScopes=true in CI catches singleton-consuming-scoped at startup.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Caches, config readers, IHttpClientFactory, stateless thread-safe services
Capturing scoped deps; mutable shared state without locks
Resolving outside request scope without CreateScope()
Lightweight stateless helpers, per-operation ID generators
Heavy allocations if resolved many times per request
Disabled in some production configs — hides bugs

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Cannot explain the rule 'longer lifetime cannot depend on shorter lifetime'. Saying DbContext can be singleton 'for performance'. Not knowing scoped = per-request in ASP.NET Core. Unable to distinguish transient (new per resolution) from scoped (new per scope).

interviewTakeaways: Three lifetimes: singleton (app), scoped (per request/scope), transient (per resolution). Shorter cannot be consumed by longer.
DbContext is always scoped — one per request, disposed at request end. Never singleton.
Production tip: dotnet-counters ActiveDbContexts; ValidateScopes in CI; load test for ObjectDisposedException.

60s: Singleton one instance app-wide. Scoped one per request scope — DbContext, tenant context. Transient new every resolve. Rule: singleton cannot inject scoped. ValidateScopes catches violations at startup.
Follow-up: why is IHttpClientFactory singleton but HttpClient instances are not?
commonPitfalls: DbContext as singleton gets you rejected immediately — EF contexts are not thread-safe and must not outlive a unit of work.
Disabling ValidateScopes in production to silence startup warnings — ships captive dependency bugs.

Strong answer: 'Scoped for per-request state like DbContext. Singleton for thread-safe shared services. Transient for cheap stateless helpers. Longer cannot depend on shorter. Monitor ActiveDbContexts in production.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: NestJS Scope.REQUEST creates a new provider instance per HTTP request — identical semantics to AddScoped. Injecting REQUEST-scoped into DEFAULT (singleton) throws at bootstrap, mirroring ValidateScopes.
Express attaches per-request state via req object or AsyncLocalStorage — manual scoped lifetime. Module-level let db = connect() is the Node equivalent of singleton capturing a scoped resource.
